newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korea honours victims of Kwangju massacre.
newsitem.headline: South Korea honours victims of Kwangju massacre.

text.p: In an emotional ceremony, South Korea on Sunday honoured as democracy fighters the mostly student victims of a 1980 army massacre in the southwestern city of Kwangju.

But historic ceremonies at a newly-dedicated cemetery attended by thousands of Kwangju residents, many of them elderly women still anguished by the loss of loved ones, were marred by student violence.
Prime Minister Koh Kun led the first ever official mourning during rites to mark the anniversary of the military rampage at the "May 18 Cemetery".

"The Kwangju massacre was a fight to protect democracy," he told relatives of the victims who streamed into the cemetery in chartered buses, aboard trucks and by foot bearing incense and gifts of fruit to the dead.
"We should not forget the tragic past," he said. "The citizens of Kwangju should show their strength to overcome the past and help spread the spirit to all Koreans."
Koh laid a single white chrysanthemum on a black marble altar in front of a 40-metre (131 foot) high memorial in the form of stylised hands clasping an egg, a symbol of life.
Nearby, Choi Kil-dong, whose 25-year-old daughter was eight months pregnant when paratroopers shot her dead, wept beside a simple tombstone that read: "You were an angel. See you in heaven."
More than 200 people died, by official count, when paratroopers stormed Kwangju to crush an armed revolt against martial law imposed by then-general Chun Doo Hwan, who later became president.
Residents say several thousand may have been killed by machinegun fire and bayonets and their bodies buried in unmarked graves or burned.
Only recently have South Koreans begun to confront the darkest chapter in their recent history, which has left deep scars to this day.
Chun was sentenced to life in jail and his presidential successor Roh Tae-woo to 17 years for their part in the carnage, after final appeals were exhausted in April.
Thousands of police cradling teargas rifles ringed the cemetery, wary of trouble after radical students from a Kwangju university fought pitched battles with officers overnight.
The students were trying to hijack the ceremonies by demanding the right to parade through the streets the coffin of a colleague who died of a heart attack during an anti-government protest in March.
Throughout the night they rained rocks and molotov cocktails on squads of riot police trying to stop them marching out of the campus, where the coffin lay draped in the national flag.
On Sunday, streets around the university were ankle-deep in rubble, smashed glass and spent teargas cannisters.
A group of about 1,000 students managed to battle their way off the college grounds and marched on the cemetery where they arrived with roars and shouts.
Police around the graves drew back to avoid spoiling the solemn funeral rites with violence. Earlier, they succeeded in blocking militant workers and farmers from bursting in.
The bodies of 124 victims were moved to the new cemetery from nearby graves this month. Relatives of 19 others have refused to rebury the remains. Other victims are listed as missing.
"What use is a new cemetery. It won't bring back my son," wailed Kim Chan-un, prostrating herself on the grave of her son who was just 17 when paratroopers shot him dead.
"The government wouldn't have had to waste money building this cemetery if they hadn't massacred innocent people in the first place."
